beginner.summary: For system administrators, network engineers, developers and support staff who use DNS every day but have never run it. Covers how a stub, recursive resolver and authoritative server cooperate, reading dig output, the namespace tree, common record types, zones, delegation and glue, SOA timers and zone transfers, TTLs and negative caching, zone files, BIND 9 as primary and secondary, reverse zones, Unbound as a caching resolver, client resolver settings on Linux and Windows, registrars and RDAP, email records, the DNS message on the wire, failure diagnosis with dig, kdig and drill, a hosted zone in Amazon Route 53, and a capstone that builds and delegates a lab domain.
prerequisites: Understands IPv4 and IPv6 addressing, UDP and TCP ports and what a default gateway does
Works confidently in a Linux shell: editing files with an editor such as vim or nano, using sudo and reading logs with journalctl
Has a Linux virtual machine or container host (Ubuntu or Debian recommended) with rights to install packages and open UDP and TCP port 53 locally
outcomes: Trace a name from the root to the authoritative answer with dig +trace and explain every referral, flag and section in the output
Write valid zone files and serve them from a BIND 9 primary and secondary pair that stay in sync through NOTIFY and IXFR
Run Unbound as a caching resolver and point Linux and Windows clients at it, then explain cache behaviour using TTLs and negative caching
Diagnose NXDOMAIN, NODATA, SERVFAIL, REFUSED, truncation and lame delegation using dig, kdig and drill and state the root cause

intermediate.summary: For engineers who already run zones and resolvers and now need to secure, automate and spread them across platforms. Covers DNSSEC records and the chain of trust, signing with BIND dnssec-policy and Knot DNS, validating with Unbound, PowerDNS Authoritative with its HTTP API, PowerDNS Recursor and dnsdist, split-horizon with BIND views and Unbound local zones, dynamic updates with TSIG, DNS over TLS, HTTPS and QUIC, Route 53 routing policies, health checks and Resolver endpoints, Azure DNS and Azure DNS Private Resolver, Google Cloud DNS, CoreDNS in Kubernetes, Active Directory DNS at awareness level, DMARC reporting and MTA-STS, DNS as code, and a capstone that serves one signed, split-horizon zone from cloud and on-premises servers.
prerequisites: Completed the beginner level or can already write zone files, run a BIND primary and secondary and diagnose failures with dig +trace
Has an account in at least one of AWS, Azure or Google Cloud with rights to create DNS zones and virtual networks, and the matching CLI installed
Can run containers with Docker and has access to a Kubernetes cluster such as kind, minikube or a managed cluster, with kubectl configured
outcomes: Sign zones with BIND and Knot DNS, publish DS records at the parent and prove validation end to end with delv and DNSViz
Serve different answers to internal and external clients with BIND views, Unbound local zones and cloud private zones without leaking internal names
Configure weighted, latency, failover and geolocation routing in Route 53 and Cloud DNS, and private resolution in Azure DNS, with health checks that move traffic on failure
Run encrypted DNS transports, CoreDNS in Kubernetes and DNS-as-code pipelines that preview and apply record changes from version control
